questions.stem: All sounds are made when something…
questions.explanation: Every sound starts with a vibration: something shaking back and forth very fast, like a drum skin or a guitar string.

questions.stem: Match each instrument to the part that vibrates.
pairs: the voice box in your throat
questions.explanation: Hitting, plucking and blowing all make a part of the instrument vibrate. When you speak, your voice box vibrates.

questions.stem: Sound can travel through water.
questions.explanation: Sound travels through gases (air), liquids (water) and solids. Whales and dolphins hear each other under water.

questions.stem: Astronauts can talk to each other in empty space without radios, because sound travels everywhere.
questions.explanation: Sound needs particles to pass the vibrations along. Space is almost empty, so sound cannot travel there. Astronauts use radios.

questions.stem: We measure how loud a sound is in ___, using a sound level ___.
questions.explanation: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB) with a sound level meter. Many mobile phones have a sound meter app.

questions.stem: Which materials would be good at blocking sound? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Soft, thick materials such as curtains, foam and wool soak up sound vibrations. Thin, hard materials like foil and glass let much more sound through.

questions.stem: Sort these into higher pitch or lower pitch.
questions.explanation: Short, thin, tight and small things vibrate faster and make higher notes. Long, loose and big things vibrate slower and make lower notes.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how you hear a school bell.
sequence: The bell is hit and vibrates.
The air next to the bell vibrates.
The vibrations travel through the air.
Your brain tells you it is a bell.
questions.explanation: The vibrating bell makes the air vibrate. The vibration passes from particle to particle until it reaches your ear, and your brain makes sense of it.

questions.stem: **Pitch** tells us how…
options: high or low a sound is
loud or quiet a sound is
questions.explanation: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. Loudness (volume) is a different thing: a high sound can be loud or quiet.

questions.stem: Put your ear on a desk while a friend taps the other end. Why do you hear the tap clearly?
questions.model_answer: Sound travels well through solids like the wooden desk, so the vibrations reach your ear clearly.
questions.explanation: Particles in a solid are close together, so they pass vibrations along very well. Sound travels better through solids than through air.

questions.stem: Materials that stop sound from travelling through them are called sound ___.
questions.explanation: Sound insulation, like foam or thick cloth, soaks up vibrations so less sound gets through.

questions.stem: An ektara player presses her finger on the string to make it shorter. What happens to the note?
questions.explanation: A shorter string vibrates faster, so the pitch goes up. Plucking harder would make it louder, not higher.

questions.stem: The bottles are tapped with a spoon. Which bottle makes the **highest** note?
questions.image_alt: Four glass bottles A to D. A has the least water and D has the most.
questions.explanation: When you tap a bottle, the glass and water vibrate. Less water means less to shake, so it vibrates faster: bottle A gives the highest note.

questions.stem: Look at the four sound pictures. Which one shows a **loud, high** sound?
questions.image_alt: Four wave drawings A to D: tall wide waves, short wide waves, tall close waves and short close waves.
questions.explanation: Taller waves mean a louder sound. Waves closer together mean a higher pitch. C has tall, close waves: loud and high.

questions.stem: Use the decibel scale. Which sound could damage your hearing if you listened for a long time?
questions.image_alt: A decibel scale from 0 to 140 with leaves 20, birds 40, talking 60, traffic 80, loud music 100 and a plane 120 dB. Above 85 dB is shaded.
questions.explanation: Sounds above about 85 dB can damage hearing. Loud music is about 100 dB, so it is in the danger zone.

questions.stem: Match each picture to how it makes a sound.
questions.explanation: Hitting, plucking, blowing and shaking are different ways of making something vibrate.

questions.stem: Two children made this string telephone. What must they do to make it work best?
questions.image_alt: Two cups joined by a long string.
options: Use a very short string with a knot in it.
Hold the string with their fingers in the middle.
questions.explanation: Vibrations travel along a tight string. A loose string, or fingers touching it, stops the vibrations.

questions.stem: A family lives next to a busy road in Dhaka. The baby cannot sleep because of the noise. What is the best thing to try first?
options: Hang thick curtains and put a rug on the floor.
Put a metal sheet on the bed.
questions.explanation: Thick, soft materials such as curtains and rugs absorb sound. Opening windows lets more noise in, and paint or metal do not soak up sound.

questions.stem: Rafi works in a factory with loud machines all day. Which advice is the most important for his health?
questions.explanation: Loud sounds above about 85 dB, heard for a long time, can damage hearing. Ear defenders block the sound.

questions.stem: Mitu says: 'The road outside the hospital is a silent zone, so drivers must not honk their horns.' Is this a sensible rule?
questions.explanation: Sick people need rest, and loud horns can harm hearing and sleep. Silent zones near hospitals and schools protect people from noise.

questions.stem: Your class wants a quiet reading corner. Which changes would help? Choose all that are right.
options: put cushions and a soft rug there
hang a cloth curtain around it
put it next to the noisy door
line one wall with egg boxes or foam
add a metal bin to drum on
questions.explanation: Soft, thick, bumpy materials absorb sound. Being next to the door, or adding something to bang, makes the corner noisier.

questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the sound when you move the **frequency** slider up?

sim.task: Open Sound Waves. Turn on the sound so you can hear the speaker. Move the frequency slider from low to high and listen. Watch the waves.

options: The sound gets louder and the waves get taller.
The pitch gets higher and the waves get closer together.
questions.explanation: Frequency is how many vibrations happen each second. More vibrations each second means a higher pitch, so the waves are drawn closer together.

questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens when you move the **amplitude** slider up?

sim.task: Open Sound Waves. Keep the frequency the same. Move the amplitude slider from low to high and listen.

questions.explanation: Amplitude is how big the vibrations are. Bigger vibrations make a louder sound, but the pitch stays the same.

questions.stem: In the simulation, when the air is removed from around the speaker, the sound becomes quieter.

sim.task: Open Sound Waves and choose the Air Pressure screen. Turn the sound on, then remove the air from around the speaker and listen.

questions.explanation: Sound needs particles to travel. With less air around the speaker, there are fewer particles to pass on the vibrations, so less sound reaches you.

questions.stem: In a thunderstorm you see the lightning before you hear the thunder, although both happen at the same time. What does this tell you?
options: Your ears work more slowly than your eyes.
The thunder happens later than the lightning.
Light travels much faster than sound.
questions.explanation: Light reaches you almost instantly, but sound travels much more slowly through air. The bigger the gap, the further away the storm.

questions.stem: Class 3C tested materials around a ringing alarm clock: none 70 dB, foil 66 dB, newspaper 60 dB, towel 50 dB, foam 45 dB. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: All the materials blocked the same amount.
Shiny materials blocked the most sound.
Soft, thick materials blocked the most sound.
Paper is the best sound insulator.
questions.explanation: Foam and the towel (soft, thick) gave the lowest readings. Foil (shiny, thin) blocked the least. The data support 'soft, thick materials block most sound'.

questions.stem: A guitar has six strings of the same length. The thickest string makes the lowest note. Explain why.
questions.model_answer: A thicker string is heavier, so it vibrates more slowly, and slower vibrations make a lower pitch.
questions.explanation: The thicker the string, the more slowly it vibrates. Fewer vibrations each second make a lower note.

questions.stem: Which word means how loud a sound is?
questions.explanation: Volume (loudness) is how loud or quiet a sound is. Pitch is how high or low it is.
